{"id": "18:19/q09", "question": "How should 'a day or part of a day' be understood?", "turns_on": "Whether aw expresses one uncertain estimate, a correction, or different speakers; one report gives longer guesses.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q09/p1", "position": "The group gave an uncertain estimate, first thinking a day and then part of one.", "reasons": "Morning entry and remaining sunlight explain the revision for Muqatil, Yahya, al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Tabrisi and others. Alusi favors plain doubt over a correction; Tabatabai says one speaker's uncertain estimate and rejects distributed speakers. Ibn Kathir says they later deferred to God. Al-Burhān's discussion of wishing distinguishes desire for an outcome from love and debates which particles can mark prospective and past senses; this gives general grammatical background to a speaker's uncertain estimate, without determining the duration."}, {"id": "18:19/q09/p2", "position": "Different youths supplied the two estimates: some said a day, others part of one.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas transmits Ibn Abbas with separate youths; Abu Hayyan allows aw to distribute the answers; Elmalili reads the two groups similarly; Ibn Ashur allows it. Alusi calls distribution unlikely; Tabatabai rejects it."}, {"id": "18:19/q09/p3", "position": "The report has one day, two days, or longer.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas report in al-Durr and Tabatabai; Tabatabai objects that two days or more conflicts with the Quranic wording and ordinary evidence."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q10", "question": "Why did their estimate seem so short, and what later made them doubt it?", "turns_on": "The sources differ on the immediate cue for the short guess and on the later evidence of elapsed time.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q10/p1", "position": "They slept from morning until later daylight, so the visible sun made a day or part of one seem plausible.", "reasons": "Yahya, Muqatil, al-Wahidi and many others describe morning entry and late waking; al-Kashifi places waking around afternoon, which Bursevi favors because a shopping round trip needed daylight. Alusi says sleep haze prevented checking signs."}, {"id": "18:19/q10/p2", "position": "Their grown hair and nails, or altered faces, suggested a much longer sleep.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi, al-Baghawi, al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Study Quran mention the signs; Ibn Jawzi reports them as an alternative. Kashshaf juxtaposes these signs with the morning account."}, {"id": "18:19/q10/p3", "position": "Sleep and inward absorption disrupt the ability to measure elapsed time.", "reasons": "Al-Baydawi says sleepers cannot measure duration; al-Qushayri says absorption removed self-awareness; Alusi says sleep haze; Tabatabai notes shadows and sunlight cannot fix an exact day and external events require indicators. Al-Damghānī's lexical heading lists falling and cessation or interruption among senses of zawāl; the excerpt does not develop those senses."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q11", "question": "Who said that their Lord knew best how long they had stayed?", "turns_on": "The repeated qālū may introduce another group, the whole group, a named leader, or divine speech.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q11/p1", "position": "A different group of youths corrected those who estimated a day.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says the others deferred; al-Zamakhshari says evidence or inspiration showed them a long stay; Abu Hayyan prefers two groups from the dialogue. Alusi says this fits its question-and-answer structure; Tabatabai says they had deeper monotheistic insight, distinct from the factions of 18:12."}, {"id": "18:19/q11/p2", "position": "Their leader Maksalmina, the eldest, stopped the dispute.", "reasons": "Muqatil names him; al-Mawardi cites Ibn Abbas; al-Tha'labi and al-Baghawi transmit this explanation; Ibn Jawzi records the name as Miksalmina."}, {"id": "18:19/q11/p3", "position": "Tamlikha or Yamlikha, described as their leader, gave the answer.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi cites Ibn Abbas; al-Tabrisi and al-Razi cite him as the leader, with al-Razi saying altered hair, nails and faces led him to infer a long period. Ibn Jawzi records a competing name. Al-Itqān identifies Tamlikhā as leader and the speaker who said God knew the duration."}, {"id": "18:19/q11/p4", "position": "The whole group agreed to defer to God, or one person's accepted answer was attributed to all.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur gives both possibilities; al-Baghawi reports the group statement; al-Biqai sees affectionate agreement. Alusi disfavors the same speaker giving both answers."}, {"id": "18:19/q11/p5", "position": "It is God's own statement about their duration.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi records this alternative to speech by the youths."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q12", "question": "What does deferring their duration to God express?", "turns_on": "The ordinary explanation concerns epistemic humility; the inward account treats time itself differently.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q12/p1", "position": "They acknowledge that only God knows the exact, long duration, and end an unresolvable dispute.", "reasons": "Muqatil says Maksalmina returns the matter to God; al-Qushayri says God placed them in that state; al-Kashshaf says signs or inspiration may have exposed their ignorance; al-Biqai calls it faithful fellowship; Tabatabai contrasts human inference from indicators with God's direct encompassing knowledge (96:5; 2:32). Sībawayh explains the hope in 20:44 as belonging to Moses and Aaron, whose knowledge of the outcome was limited; this supplies a parallel for speech limited to human knowledge."}, {"id": "18:19/q12/p2", "position": "A leader urged them to stop disagreement because it can ruin a community.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas transmits Ibn Abbas through Sa'id b. Jubayr; al-Durr repeats the leader's warning."}, {"id": "18:19/q12/p3", "position": "Some spiritually realized sleepers understood that the interval had no independent reality.", "reasons": "Asad connects this to 18:12 and death and resurrection."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q13", "question": "How many youths does the dialogue imply?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q13/p1", "position": "At least seven: one asks and two plural replies require three speakers each.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafi attributes the inference to Ibn Abbas; Tabatabai gives the same count from the singular and two plurals."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q14", "question": "Why do they turn from duration to sending for food?", "turns_on": "Both hunger and fear shape the errand.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q14/p1", "position": "They woke hungry and redirected an unknowable discussion to an immediate need.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says they needed food; al-Kashshaf, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur call the pivot wiser than continuing debate; al-Qushayri says hunger followed a period without bodily appetites; Alusi points to fa as marking the redirect. Al-Rāzī's general account distinguishes ends desired in themselves from means, assigns appetite its own pleasure, and says perceived pleasure draws action unless a stronger consideration intervenes; his examples include tasty food avoided for harm and immediate pain accepted to escape worse harm."}, {"id": "18:19/q14/p2", "position": "The errand also let the envoy learn news about their pursuers.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari and al-Tha'labi report instructions to buy more food and investigate; they still believed Decianus sought them."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q15", "question": "Who was sent to the city?", "turns_on": "Narrative reports name the envoy; the verse leaves him unnamed.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q15/p1", "position": "Yamlikha, also called Tamlikha, was the envoy.", "reasons": "Muqatil names Yamliha; al-Tabari transmits Muqatil and narrative forms; al-Tha'labi, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and others give variants. Al-Ghaznawi calls him the youngest; al-Wahidi has their leader Tamlikha speak earlier. Al-Damghānī names the envoy Malyakhā; al-Itqān names him Tamlikhā."}, {"id": "18:19/q15/p2", "position": "An unnamed member of their group went; the command need not identify him.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the group may address an unspecified delegate or omit the known name; the Quran's 'one of you' emphasizes membership."}, {"id": "18:19/q15/p3", "position": "The wording 'one of you' avoids suggesting a specially honored chief.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbari contrasts aḥad with wāḥid; Alusi says the latter might imply their chief. Abū Ḥātim supplies wider lexical reasons for the choice of aḥad over wāḥid: its scope, gender invariance, collective possibility and restricted arithmetic use."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q16", "question": "How does 'with your silver' attach to the envoy?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q16/p1", "position": "It is circumstantial to 'one of you': the envoy goes carrying the silver.", "reasons": "Al-Samin describes the prepositional phrase as a circumstantial qualifier."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q17", "question": "What occupations do reports give the youths?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q17/p1", "position": "They were money changers.", "reasons": "Abu Ja'far's report calls them money changers; al-Sadiq distinguishes changers in speech from dealers in coins."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q18", "question": "What is 'your silver'?", "turns_on": "Whether the noun denotes silver generally or minted coins in its lexical scope.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q18/p1", "position": "Silver, whether struck as dirhams or unminted; in context it was their money.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba and later authors cite the Arfaja silver-nose report to show unminted silver is included. {"id": "18:19/q19", "question": "How is bi-wariqikum read?", "turns_on": "The variants concern vowel easing and the qāf-kāf contact; sources disagree on which assimilations are sound.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q19/p1", "position": "Fatḥa on wāw and sukūn on rāʾ lightens pronunciation.", "reasons": "Al-Farra names Asim and al-A'mash; most Kufans/Basrans, Abu Amr, Hamza and Abu Bakr are often named. Ibn Khalawayh, al-Nahhas and Qiraat-Er explain avoiding a heavy sequence of vowels. Ibn al-Jazarī names Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza, Khalaf, Abū Bakr and Rawḥ as leaving the rāʾ of biwariqikum unvocalized."}, {"id": "18:19/q19/p2", "position": "Assimilation of qāf into kāf, sometimes with a still rāʾ, is transmitted.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari reports a Meccan form; al-Zajjaj permits it and al-Farisi explains movement from the rear qāf to nearer kāf. Abu Hatim transmits Ibn Muhaysin; Ibn Jinni says possible, yet calls Abu Raja's form concealed articulation rather than full assimilation because full assimilation transfers the vowel. Abu Hayyan challenges a reported attribution to Ibn Kathir. Ibn al-Jazarī reports two valid treatments of a quiescent qāf before kāf: Makkī retains its emphatic quality, while al-Dānī assimilates fully; Ibn al-Jazarī favors the latter by analogy with a moving qāf and warns against weakening an unassimilated qāf. He limits within-word qāf-to-kāf assimilation to forms with a moving preceding letter and following plural mīm."}, {"id": "18:19/q19/p3", "position": "Fatḥa on wāw and kasra on rāʾ, with qāf pronounced, is the common or original reading.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari prefers the original kasra pattern but accepts alternatives; Ibn Khalawayh calls kasra original. Ibn Mujahid, al-Farisi, al-Qurtubi and others name Ibn Kathir, Nafi, Ibn Amir, al-Kisa'i and Hafs; al-Tabari lists Medinan and some Iraqi readers. The forms are Arabic dialect variants with the same sense. Ibn al-Jazarī explicitly lists biwariqikum among forms where qāf is pronounced distinctly, because its preceding letter is quiescent; he reports kasra on rāʾ for the remaining readers."}, {"id": "18:19/q19/p4", "position": "Kasra on wāw, with varying rāʾ and assimilation, is a rare dialectal reading.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj judges kasra wāw least acceptable; al-Farra compares kibid and kalima. Ibn Jinni treats Abu Raja's form as concealed articulation; Zamakhshari and Razi object to two consecutive still letters in Ibn Muhaysin's form; Abu Hayyan cites a nonassimilated Zajjaj form."}, {"id": "18:19/q19/p5", "position": "Ali reads bawāriqikum, a collective form relating to silver.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Samin describe its pattern; Alusi mentions it."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q20", "question": "What does the demonstrative 'this' add to the silver?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q20/p1", "position": "It points to money at hand, perhaps held out or handed to the envoy.", "reasons": "Bursevi infers a companion physically handed it over; Alusi says the speaker held it out. Tabatabai says the unusually emphatic mention foreshadows how the aged coin exposed them. Sībawayh observes that an identified person may be indicated by a bare proper name when a visible sign reveals him, as if 'this' were uttered; this supplies a general Arabic parallel for demonstrative pointing."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q21", "question": "What were the coins like and where had they come from?", "turns_on": "Narratives add the old ruler's imprint to the verse's bare mention of silver.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q21/p1", "position": "They carried old coins from the reign they fled, often bearing the persecuting king's image.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi and Ibn Abbas say the stamped image was the old king's; al-Tabari dates the coins 309 years earlier; al-Tha'labi says Daqyanus' seal. Ibn Kathir says they brought and spent money when fleeing; Abu Hayyan says they brought it for expenses. Ibn Abbas likens the currency to camel hooves; later reports call the ruler Decius."}, {"id": "18:19/q21/p2", "position": "Their coin was silver but its exact minting is not specified by the verse.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, al-Kashshaf and al-Razi allow coined and uncoined silver; al-Wahidi cites the old stamped-coin narrative as a separate report."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q22", "question": "Which city was meant?", "turns_on": "Reports vary in names and whether they denote one city over time.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q22/p1", "position": "Their former city was Ephesus, also reported as Daqsus or Daphsus and later called Tarsus.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari calls it Ephesus; al-Wahidi calls it Daqsus and present Tarsus; al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi and Alusi reconcile Ephesus as the former name with Tarsus as later name. Alusi says it was familiar home; Ibn Ashur calls it Ephesus. Al-Tha'labi's story spells Daphsus. Ibn al-Jawzī reports that some exegetes call it the youths' town and Muqātil names it Ephesus."}, {"id": "18:19/q22/p2", "position": "Tarsus is the city's name.", "reasons": "Several sources state this directly without reconciling the older name."}, {"id": "18:19/q22/p3", "position": "It was the city from which they fled; its specific name is unnecessary to the phrase.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi and Ibn Kathir identify it by relation to the youths; the Quran leaves the proper name unstated."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q23", "question": "Who or what does 'which of it' refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the city's people, its locations, or its foods are supplied to resolve the pronoun.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q23/p1", "position": "The city's inhabitants or vendors are understood: which person has the relevant food.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas supply 'people'; al-Kashshaf compares 'ask the town' at 12:82; al-Nasafi, al-Samin, Bursevi and Tabatabai agree. Al-Tabari notes listeners understand food belongs to people."}, {"id": "18:19/q23/p2", "position": "The pronoun can point directly to foods understood from context.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas allows 'which food'; al-Samin says no elision is required; Abu Hayyan and Alusi present this alternative."}, {"id": "18:19/q23/p3", "position": "It can refer grammatically to the city itself with an understood person or place.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says the syntax attaches it to 'city' although the sense is inhabitants; Alusi lists city, residents, or food."}, {"id": "18:19/q23/p4", "position": "It means which place in the city, such as a market stall.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur makes place the referent and ṭaʿāman the specification of the comparative."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q24", "question": "How is 'let him look which has purer food' parsed?", "turns_on": "The grammatical choice is interrogative versus relative ayyu and whether naẓar governs it or its clause.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q24/p1", "position": "Ayyuhā is an interrogative subject, azkā its predicate, and ṭaʿāman a specification.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj gives this parse; al-Wahidi cites Abu Ishaq; al-Razi and al-Nasafi follow; al-Samin and Alusi allow it. Al-Burhān reports al-Saʿdī's and grammarians' differing rules for a comparative annexed to its genus, then identifies azkā ṭaʿāman as a tamyīz construction scholars must explain within those rules. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the specification explicitly states the criterion of comparison, unlike an unqualified superlative. Sībawayh requires a predicate after the interrogative subject within this embedded question: the question cannot depend on what precedes it and must be completed by what follows."}, {"id": "18:19/q24/p2", "position": "Ayy may be relative and function as the object, with an omitted predicate.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan attributes this to Sibawayh; al-Samin and Alusi record the interrogative/relative options."}, {"id": "18:19/q24/p3", "position": "The interrogative clause is what 'let him look' investigates.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash says naẓar can be followed by a question without directly governing ayyu, illustrated with 'look, is Zayd more generous or Amr?'; al-Tabrisi calls the whole clause the object. Sībawayh says the interrogative clause in 'let him look which has purer food' occupies the verb's object position while retaining independent internal syntax, as at 18:12. He distinguishes direct government when no question intervenes, illustrates other embedded-question positions and accusative Arab usage, and notes that intransitive naẓar and asking about someone leave the name within the question. Al-Itqān says the exegete must attend to particles, nouns, verbs and adverbs because their varying uses alter meaning and inference. Sībawayh says the interrogative hamza prevents the preceding verb from governing the internal nominal clause in 'which has purer food'; he contrasts a question beginning the complement, whose subject stays nominative, with an independently framed question later governed by a verb. He explains that araʾaytuka takes an accusative first object and the interrogative clause as its second object. His comparisons distinguish accusative adverbial 'which day' from nominative nonadverbial use, note Arabs' varying case for 'which time,' and cite a poetic 'in every state or time' as adverbial. Al-Itqān gives ʿinda as a separate example of a word used only adverbially or governed by min; this is general background on grammatical government, not a gloss on a word in this verse."}, {"id": "18:19/q24/p4", "position": "Naẓar can mean seeing or mental consideration.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan states both senses."}]}

Al-Tabari prefers lawful food over mere abundance regardless of seller's stock. Ibn Kathir invokes 24:21 and 87:14 for purity and prefers wholesome purity. Reports also mention slaughtered pigs. Al-Damghānī glosses azkā in the sleepers' request as 'more lawful.'"}, {"id": "18:19/q25/p2", "position": "The more abundant food, or the vendor with the most food.", "reasons": "Ikrima gives the gloss; Abu Ubayda cites the seven-versus-three tribes line, repeated by al-Tha'labi; Ibn Qutayba derives it from increase. Al-Tabari accepts this Arabic usage but says it does not decide the context and prefers lawful purity."}, {"id": "18:19/q25/p3", "position": "The tastiest, most pleasant, or wholesome food.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi give taste; Ibn Kathir prefers a wholesome/pure sense supported by purification verses, while distinguishing it from mere quantity."}, {"id": "18:19/q25/p4", "position": "The better or finest food in quality.", "reasons": "Qatada gives this repeatedly; Muqatil ibn Hayyan gives best quality. Alusi judges Qatada's reading best; Ibn Ashur argues zakā conveys increased goodness and benefit."}, {"id": "18:19/q25/p5", "position": "The cheaper food or best value.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba lists low price; al-Mawardi, Ibn Jawzi and Yaman ibn Ri'ab give it, and al-Kashshaf, al-Nasafi, Baydawi and Bursevi include it."}, {"id": "18:19/q25/p6", "position": "Lawful food specifically means food not stolen, extorted, usurped or bought with injustice.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj offers the source-of-property sense; Mujahid links it to an oppressive ruler's markets; al-Dahhak says much local property was seized. Abu Ishaq combines this with lawful slaughter; al-Wahidi states both."}, {"id": "18:19/q25/p7", "position": "More blessed or fruitful food.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Qurtubi preserve this gloss; Alusi says zakā's increase may be otherworldly reward from lawfulness or material benefit."}, {"id": "18:19/q25/p8", "position": "A gloss transmitted as arfaḍ.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi ascribes the wording to Yaman b. Ri'ab without further explanation."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q26", "question": "What specific food did they seek or buy?", "turns_on": "Reports name different foods while the verse keeps the noun general.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q26/p1", "position": "Lawfully slaughtered meat, perhaps from a concealed believer.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, Sa'id and al-Farra point to Magian or idolatrous slaughter; al-Kashifi says hidden believers could supply meat."}, {"id": "18:19/q26/p2", "position": "Raisins.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya transmits this possibility; Abu Hayyan and Alusi list it among proposed foods."}, {"id": "18:19/q26/p3", "position": "Dates.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya gives it as an alternative to raisins; Abu Hayyan and Alusi also list it."}, {"id": "18:19/q26/p4", "position": "Rice.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Alusi list it."}, {"id": "18:19/q26/p5", "position": "Enough food for several people, without a specified item.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi adds the group's quantity to the generic noun."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q27", "question": "What does 'bring you provision from it' mean?", "turns_on": "The antecedent of minhu may be selected food or the coins; both yield provisions.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q27/p1", "position": "Bring them some of the selected food for them to eat.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari's report and al-Mawardi give food; al-Tha'labi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Ashur call it sustenance. Tabatabai prefers the antecedent 'food' because silver would require an extra omitted pronoun."}, {"id": "18:19/q27/p2", "position": "Bring lawful food for them to eat.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi records a more specific gloss; Alusi says the provision should be lawful on either pronoun analysis."}, {"id": "18:19/q27/p3", "position": "The pronoun 'from it' can refer to their silver, the source or substitute for the provision.", "reasons": "Alusi allows min to be partitive, source marking or substitution; Tabatabai calls this remote because an additional pronoun must be assumed."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q28", "question": "What does 'let him act gently' require?", "turns_on": "The verb's gentleness is applied to concealment, buying, seller relations, or the food's delicacy.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q28/p1", "position": "Move, shop and return discreetly, carefully and courteously so their presence stays hidden.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Yahya stress secrecy; al-Tabari, al-Tha'labi, al-Baghawi, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir specify roads, entry and purchases. Abu Hayyan prefers concealment from context; Tabatabai specifies smooth dealing to prevent quarrels and rejects generic transaction caution. Alusi includes courtesy; al-Qushayri emphasizes kind dealing with the seller."}, {"id": "18:19/q28/p2", "position": "Bargain or inspect carefully to avoid a high price or being cheated.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi gives low-price bargaining; al-Kashshaf, al-Nasafi and Baydawi give avoiding deception. Tabatabai argues this broad transactional sense lacks support from the following secrecy clause."}, {"id": "18:19/q28/p3", "position": "Deal gently with the seller without haggling or quarrelling.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi offers this alternative; al-Qushayri and Alusi stress courtesy, and Tabatabai says a quarrel could betray them."}, {"id": "18:19/q28/p4", "position": "Choose delicate food suited to recently fasting bodies or refined spiritual people.", "reasons": "Alusi records the bodily and spiritual explanations but rejects making delicate food a rule, citing simple diet and clothing of the Prophet and major Companions."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q29", "question": "How are the commands 'let him look' and 'let him act gently' read?", "turns_on": "The variation is vowel on the imperative lām and an attested passive verb.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q29/p1", "position": "The command lām is quiescent in the common reading; kasra preserves its original vowel.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj allows kasra in falyatikum; al-Nahhas notes it in li-ya'tikum and li-yatalaṭṭaf; Ibn Atiyya reports al-Hasan's kasra in falyanẓur and yatalattaf; al-Samin calls it original. Ibn al-Jazarī's general recitation rules distinguish clear quiescent lām before nūn, solar-letter assimilation, the agreed assimilation in qul rabbī, and cross-word assimilation; he also reports an exceptional emphatic lām in thalātha, standard treatment of Allah's lām, and rejects al-Ahwāzī's anomalous contrary report."}, {"id": "18:19/q29/p2", "position": "Qutayba al-Mayyal reads yutalaṭṭaf passively, with ḍamma on yāʾ.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and Alusi report it."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q30", "question": "What does 'let him not alert anyone to you' mean?", "turns_on": "The warning's scope differs when the envoy is captured.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q30/p1", "position": "He must tell no one about the group or its location and avoid conduct that reveals them.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba derive shaʿara as knowing and connect 'poet' to perception; Ibn Ashur explains causative ishʿār and an omitted object that covers their existence, number and location; the emphatic nūn signals the danger. Al-Kashshaf, al-Nasafi, Bursevi and al-Biqai include unintended disclosure. Al-Damghānī's heading lists a king's cupbearer as another possible referent of aḥad, but the excerpt supplies no example for that identification."}, {"id": "18:19/q30/p2", "position": "If he is caught, he must not expose his companions.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj, al-Tha'labi and Abu Ishaq construe the warning as protection of the others after the envoy is discovered. Al-Wahidi prefers that he not disclose them voluntarily, but reports a contrary oath if captured."}, {"id": "18:19/q30/p3", "position": "If captured, he should guide captors to the other youths so they share martyrdom.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi and others report their pledge not to keep martyrdom to one person; al-Wahidi finds this more fitting than Abu Ishaq's reading while preferring voluntary secrecy."}, {"id": "18:19/q30/p4", "position": "Here 'anyone' specifically denotes Diqyanus, the persecuting ruler.", "reasons": "Al-Damghānī identifies aḥad in the concealment warning with Diqyanus."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q31", "question": "How is 'let no one know' read grammatically?", "turns_on": "The variant changes the verb's subject and case of aḥad.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q31/p1", "position": "Abu Salih, Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa', Qutayba and Abu Ja'far read an active form with aḥad nominative as subject.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and Alusi report this reading."}, {"id": "18:19/q31/p2", "position": "The regular construction forbids the envoy to make anyone aware of them.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur calls ishʿār a causative verb taking one object and notes the emphatic nūn; al-Kashshaf says the envoy can cause awareness even unintentionally. Abū Ḥātim's lexical comparison says aḥad is more exhaustive than wāḥid, normally human-specific in absence statements, usable for one or many and invariant for gender; he contrasts their affirmative uses, plurals and arithmetic behavior, citing 112:1, 33:32 and 69:47."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q32", "question": "How did the cave open and the sleepers awaken in the narrative reports?", "turns_on": "Reports differ over how the sealed entrance was opened and include a separate later revival story.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q32/p1", "position": "A shepherd opened the cave as shelter for sheep; the youths awoke the following morning.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari attributes this to Wahb; Study Quran transmits it from al-Tabari; Ibn Atiyya records a shepherd as one account."}, {"id": "18:19/q32/p2", "position": "The entrance had been sealed, collapsed, or later unseal

ed.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi says Decianus sealed it and Tamlikha noticed the stones removed; Ibn Atiyya says it may have collapsed, alternatively been opened by a shepherd."}, {"id": "18:19/q32/p3", "position": "They awoke after the persecuting king and city had disappeared.", "reasons": "Al-Sadiq's account says the dog slept with them; al-Mawardi also reports Muqatil's statement that the dog slept."}, {"id": "18:19/q32/p4", "position": "Olyas removed stones to make a sheep pen; the revived youths greeted each other and prayed.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says terror kept others at a distance while they revived unchanged; the account gives a named agent of the opening."}, {"id": "18:19/q32/p5", "position": "God restored their souls for a later greeting to Muhammad's companions, then they returned to sleep.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi reports the four Companions brought by Solomon's wind; a variant says the Mahdi will later greet and revive them."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q33", "question": "What did the youths say and fear immediately after awakening?", "turns_on": "Narratives differ in post-awakening details and the state in which the youths were later found.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q33/p1", "position": "They simply estimated their sleep and made a food errand under a later just or Muslim king.", "reasons": "Abd Allah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr and Ibn Abbas reports describe a just or Muslim ruler already reigning."}, {"id": "18:19/q33/p2", "position": "They prayed and thought Decianus still sought them; some urged steadfastness even unto death.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari's account says Yemliha warned of forced sacrifice or death and Maksalimina vowed fidelity; al-Tha'labi reports the same with Tamlikha. Their pledge held them together in life and death."}, {"id": "18:19/q33/p3", "position": "One report has the sleepers' souls gone when the king found their bodies; another says bones had vanished.", "reasons": "Qatada reports bodies without souls; Ibn Abbas says their bones had vanished after more than 300 years. {"id": "18:19/q34", "question": "What happened when the envoy reached the changed city?", "turns_on": "Reports agree on a changed era and an old coin, but differ in officials, discovery details and the cave's outcome.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q34/p1", "position": "His ancient coin led sellers to suspect hidden treasure and take him before the authorities.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari names governors Arius/Areus and Astius; al-Tha'labi calls the first Armos. They bound or threatened him; no one knew him or his father. He asked about Decianus, learned he had died centuries earlier, and revealed companions in the cave. Ibn Abbas's report adds a baker and a scholar matching names to an old tablet."}, {"id": "18:19/q34/p2", "position": "A righteous king or governors recognized the youths as a divine sign and went to the cave.", "reasons": "Wahb and Ikrima name a just or Muslim king; al-Tabari's narrative has Areus, Astius and the people accompany Yemliha; al-Tha'labi has Armos; reports differ whether terror prevented entry, whether they found preserved bodies, and whether a mosque or church was built (18:21)."}, {"id": "18:19/q34/p3", "position": "He saw public Christian signs and heard Jesus invoked, unlike the persecution he remembered.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari and al-Tha'labi describe his bewilderment and fear of madness; Ibn Atiyya says landmarks and clothing had changed. Al-Sadiq adds mutually unintelligible speech."}, {"id": "18:19/q34/p4", "position": "The verse leaves the exact route of discovery unspecified.", "reasons": "Islahi says investigation eventually exposed their origins, perhaps through the market; Tabatabai says the old coin is a narrative key."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q35", "question": "Why did God awaken the youths in that era according to the reports?", "turns_on": "The reports supply a specific royal crisis behind the broader resurrection lesson.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q35/p1", "position": "Their awakening was a sign of resurrection and God's protection, whether or not a king had prayed.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi likens it to resurrection; Kashshaf, Baydawi, Biqai, Ibn Ashur, Study Quran and Kuranyolu emphasize divine power. Tabatabai says persecution had passed and monotheists could receive the sign."}, {"id": "18:19/q35/p2", "position": "Their appearance answered a dispute over resurrection of body and soul.", "reasons": "Ikrima says the community was divided; Ibn Ishaq names Theodosius, whose 68-year reign saw deniers of bodily resurrection gain ground. The king donned sackcloth, sat in ashes and prayed. God made the youths a sign confirming the Hour and bodily resurrection, preserving the king and believers. Al-Kashifi's version names Tindrous."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q36", "question": "What happened in the report of Muhammad's message to the sleepers?", "turns_on": "The later visitation reports differ in visitor and timing.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q36/p1", "position": "Four eminent companions carried Muhammad's greeting; the revived youths accepted his prophethood and returned to sleep.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi reports Gabriel instructing Muhammad to send Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali and Abu Dharr on a cloth carried by Solomon's gentle wind. The dog greeted them; God restored the youths' souls; they answered, praised God, accepted Islam and sent greetings. A separate variant gives the Mahdi a later greeting. The Prophet prayed for loved ones and companions."}, {"id": "18:19/q36/p2", "position": "The Mahdi will greet them, after which they will sleep until resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi presents this as a variant to the four-companion narrative."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q37", "question": "What legal rule about sending an agent is drawn from the errand?", "turns_on": "Jurists agree on delegation for need but differ over an unexcused, present principal.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q37/p1", "position": "Agency is valid for delegable, lawful matters, including buying food.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya cites Ali appointing Aqil before Uthman; al-Qurtubi adds 9:60, 12:93, Urwa al-Bariqi, Jabir collecting fifteen wasqs at Khaybar, and Bukhari's Abd al-Rahman–Umayya protection contract. Ibn al-Arabi calls this passage the strongest proof. Al-Qurtubi bars agency for usurpation or unlawful acts. Ibn ʿĀshūr explicitly uses the youths' appointment of an envoy as an example of legal inference from Quranic narrative; he compares deriving guarantee or reward contracts from Joseph's story at 12:72."}, {"id": "18:19/q37/p2", "position": "Even a healthy present person may appoint an agent.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi says most permit this and cites the Prophet delegating repayment of a camel debt with a better camel; the creditor praised the repayment."}, {"id": "18:19/q37/p3", "position": "A present person without an excuse may not appoint an agent.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi reports Abu Hanifa and Sahnun; Ibn al-Arabi speculates Sahnun used the restriction against oppressors. Al-Qurtubi and the prophetic camel report oppose it."}, {"id": "18:19/q37/p4", "position": "The youths' fear of discovery was an excuse for delegation.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi says all scholars agree an excused person may appoint an agent, even where they dispute healthy present persons."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q38", "question": "Does the shared silver support pooling money and food?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural possessive establishes shared ownership or merely a pooled errand.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q38/p1", "position": "Yes: companions may pool costs, buy jointly and eat together despite unequal appetites.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi calls this munahada; Ibn Khuwayz Mindad cites this verse and 2:220; al-Qurtubi cites school permission to mix donated meals and the orphan and shared eating verses (2:220, cited as 24:16). Al-Kiya permits an eater to pay extra for a portion."}, {"id": "18:19/q38/p2", "position": "Their communal purse expresses mutual care and rebukes habitual begging.", "reasons": "Alusi says one youth may have had no money, perhaps a shepherd, yet the group calls it theirs; Tabatabai sees equal delegation and mutual concern."}, {"id": "18:19/q38/p3", "position": "The verse alone does not prove a partnership, since each might have handed over money separately.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Arabi relies instead on hadiths. Ibn Umar's two-dates prohibition concerns companions' permission; al-Qurtubi says the army-of-khabt report may reflect equal distribution, so its joint-eating proof is weaker."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q39", "question": "What does their carrying provisions teach about trust in God?", "turns_on": "The dispute concerns ordinary means versus exceptional abandonment by those held to have special certainty.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q39/p1", "position": "Prudent provisioning and work are compatible with reliance on God.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf cites Aisha on a pilgrim's money belt and an ascetic scholar's refusal of patrons; al-Razi and Ibn Kathir agree. Bursevi cites the Mathnawi: cultivate before relying; Alusi invokes tying the camel. Abu Hayyan and al-Nasafi repeat the money belt maxim."}, {"id": "18:19/q39/p2", "position": "Those especially firm in certainty may relinquish ordinary means.", "reasons": "Alusi records eminent scholars who cite Khalid drinking poison and other extraordinary reports; Ahmad, Ishaq and others permit desert travel without supplies or foregoing earning and treatment. Abraham's refusal of Gabriel's help illustrates direct reliance. Alusi rejects attributing this only to Sufis."}]}

{"id": "18:19/q41", "question": "How is this scene linked to resurrection and the perception of time?", "turns_on": "The parallel may serve bodily resurrection, Barzakh perception, or a wider lesson on the nature of time.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q41/p1", "position": "The youths' brief estimate parallels the revived passerby and people at resurrection or in Barzakh.", "reasons": "Elmalili cites 2:259; Study Quran lists 2:259, 10:45, 17:52, 20:104, 23:112–13, 30:55, 46:35 and 79:46. {"id": "18:19/q42", "question": "What inward reading is given to their duration and awakening?", "turns_on": "The notes read the temporal disorientation as a spiritual state.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q42/p1", "position": "Spiritual awakening follows absorption; apparent time vanishes in love or union.", "reasons": "Qashani reads the youths as faculties awakening to discuss latent truths; al-Qushayri says self-absorption removes detailed awareness and cites poetry on short-feeling union; Ibn Ata says longing makes any union seem short. {"id": "18:19/q43", "question": "What do the silver, city and food signify inwardly?", "turns_on": "The allegorical mappings differ: knowledge, intellect, or scrupulous livelihood.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q43/p1", "position": "Silver is innate first principles, the city a gathering place of knowledge, and food sound knowledge that nourishes the heart.", "reasons": "Qashani cites the saying that Muhammad is the city of knowledge and Ali its gate; he rejects empty dialectic and superficial appearances, with 88:7 as a contrast. One learner may then teach the rest, as 9:122 suggests."}, {"id": "18:19/q43/p2", "position": "The envoy is thought among spiritual faculties, seeking intellect instead of illusion, imagination or sensation.", "reasons": "Qashani gives this alternate symbolic mapping of youths and city."}, {"id": "18:19/q43/p3", "position": "Pure food signifies scrupulous lawful sustenance that preserves insight.", "reasons": "Alusi quotes Dhu al-Nun on not extinguishing gnosis with scruple; he criticizes a shaykh accepting money known to come from an oppressor."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q44", "question": "What inward instruction is drawn from acting gently and concealing the youths?", "turns_on": "The inward application concerns spiritual training and the audience for hidden knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q44/p1", "position": "Choose an upright, verified guide and deal gently with spiritually mature people.", "reasons": "Qashani warns against pretenders; Sulami transmits Abu Uthman that gnostics receive gentleness and novices firmness; Yusuf ibn al-Husayn gives gnostics delicate food and ascetics ordinary food. Qushayri reports the same food distinction. Alusi criticizes a mandatory delicate-food rule because major exemplars lived simply."}, {"id": "18:19/q44/p2", "position": "Conceal spiritual realities from people unable to receive them.", "reasons": "Qashani says ignorant people should not be told the youths' state or faith; Alusi says veiled people cannot perceive such light."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q45", "question": "Why must discovery be avoided, and what threat follows?", "turns_on": "Sources parse the danger as discovery followed by bodily or verbal attack and coercion.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q45/p1", "position": "The youths feared being found by persecutors, stoned, or forced back to idolatry.", "reasons": "Yahya and the narrative sources say discovery would destroy their religious success; Tabatabai says stoning signals collective hostility. Abu Hayyan prefers literal stoning over verbal abuse and says 'return' can mean entering an old creed even without earlier membership. Tabatabai says forced participation, not merely verbal assent, was feared."}, {"id": "18:19/q45/p2", "position": "The next verse's 'appearance over you' can mean discovering their location or gaining ascendancy.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan gives both; Tabatabai cites al-Raghib's semantic path from visibility to finding and prevailing, preferring location discovery because it leads to capture."}, {"id": "18:19/q45/p3", "position": "The threatened rajm can mean verbal abuse.", "reasons": "Hajjaj and Ibn Jubayr are reported with this gloss; Abu Hayyan favors stoning because the king meant to kill and earlier people used it against dissent."}, {"id": "18:19/q45/p4", "position": "Someone trapped under coercion may outwardly comply while preserving faith, but a person free to leave must avoid voluntarily losing religious practice.", "reasons": "Tabatabai cites 16:106 and 3:28 for coerced dissimulation, 4:97 against self-imposed helplessness, and rejects proposed explanations that coercion itself causes apostasy or that dissimulation was once barred."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q46", "question": "How do later variant readings shape the threatened discovery?", "turns_on": "The following verse's verb has an active/passive variant and disputed pronoun antecedent.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q46/p1", "position": "Zayd ibn Ali reads yuẓhirū passively in the following threat.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports this reading as a continuation of the secrecy warning."}, {"id": "18:19/q46/p2", "position": "The ordinary active form means the city people find or overpower the youths.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says the pronoun may denote inferred unbelievers, generic aḥad, or elided townspeople; al-Zamakhshari favors the townspeople, invoking 23:8 for plural after a generic."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q47", "question": "What does the scene show about the youths' fellowship?", "turns_on": "The notes draw communal ethics and an inward pedagogy from the plural dialogue.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q47/p1", "position": "They share inquiry, resources, responsibility and concern for one another's faith and safety.", "reasons": "Al-Biqai sees affectionate agreement in deferring knowledge to God; Tabatabai highlights equal delegation, communal money and tact. Alusi reads 'your silver' as shared even if one youth had none, and the narratives recall their pledge never to abandon each other."}, {"id": "18:19/q47/p2", "position": "One fully developed member can learn on behalf of the group and awaken the others.", "reasons": "Qashani appeals to 9:122 for the sufficiency of one envoy in learning."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q48", "question": "How does the verse fit the surah's structure?", "turns_on": "The sources emphasize either the local narrative expansion or the larger surah purpose.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q48/p1", "position": "It expands the earlier compressed cave account and answers the surah's central challenge about resurrection.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan links the sleep-and-awakening sequence to 18:11; Islahi says the present questioning expands the summary near 18:13; al-Biqai ties the story to Quraysh's consultation of Jewish questioners and says acceptance or denial of the sign exposes whether they seek guidance. Ibn Ashur calls the Cave and Dhu al-Qarnayn stories the surah's main purposes. Ibn ʿĀshūr describes Quranic stories as teaching the history of divine law, consequences of faith and wrongdoing, virtue, historical awareness, breadth of other nations, collective ambition, and eloquent dialogue as part of inimitability; he cites 3:146, 27:52, 7:176, 12:111, 21:105, 14:45 and 41:15."}, {"id": "18:19/q48/p2", "position": "The discourse here summarizes the questioning and then supplies its words.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur and Alusi describe the summary-dialogue relation; Abu Hayyan says the surah first summarizes the episode and later retells it."}]}

{"id": "18:19/q50", "question": "How reliable and complete are the historical cave reports?", "turns_on": "The extant narratives supply different historical details, and the Quran does not settle them.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q50/p1", "position": "The reports disagree extensively, and the Quran selects only details needed for guidance.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya deliberately shortens conflicting accounts to sounder essentials. Tabatabai lists conflicting names, dates, lineage, rulers, occupations and cave sites; he attributes variation to the tale's spread among People of the Book and to Muslim uptake of converts' outside reports, including Wahb and Ka'b. He says the Quran omits biography and gives withdrawal, sleep, awakening, exposure and mosque in sequence. Ibn ʿĀshūr says Quranic stories select lessons about faith and divine care rather than ancestry or place; this city stays unnamed because the awakening, arrival and ensuing discovery confirming God's promise are the relevant events. Al-Wāḥidī requires witnessed transmission for occasions of revelation; Ibn Sīrīn reports ʿUbayda's warning that those who knew the occasions had gone. Ibn Taymiyya and al-Zarkashī distinguish a true reported occasion from a case merely included under a verse."}, {"id": "18:19/q50/p2", "position": "The broader story includes a later encounter with the cave or its remains.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari reports Ibn Abbas passing a cave whose bones had vanished; Study Quran reports another account of preserved bodies after a renewed sleep."}, {"id": "18:19/q50/p3", "position": "Christian accounts and Muslim reports partly overlap but differ on numbers, dog and duration.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says most historians place events between Jesus and Muhammad, outside the two Testaments, while Christian preservation was extensive; he compares Christian accounts with Ibn Ishaq's report."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q51", "question": "Where was the cave located according to later identifications?", "turns_on": "Archaeological and historical fit is debated without decisive identification.", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q51/p1", "position": "Rujayb near Amman is the strongest proposed fit, though identification remains unproved.", "reasons": "Tabatabai points to Jordanian excavation and some Muslim reports while stating no proposed cave has decisive evidence; he places Amman at ancient Philadelphia under Roman control until Muslim conquest."}, {"id": "18:19/q51/p2", "position": "Other proposals place it near Damascus, Petra, Scandinavia or Nakhchivan.", "reasons": "Tabatabai lists Mount Qasiyun, Petra, seven preserved Roman-looking bodies in Scandinavia and a Caucasus cave; he objects that the northern claims conflict with the Roman setting and reach."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q52", "question": "How should differing transmitted recitations relevant to this verse be treated?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q52/p1", "position": "Transmitted variants are read as taught; dispute over an accepted reading is discouraged.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd reports the Prophet rebuking a quarrel over a surah's verse count and directing readers to read as taught; Zayd ibn Arqam reports ʿAlī accepting the readings taught by Ibn Masʿūd, Zayd and Ubayy; ʿUmar reports the Prophet validating both his and Hishām's recitations and mentioning seven aḥruf."}]}
{"id": "18:19/q53", "question": "What is the form and etymology of 'the city'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q53/p1", "position": "Madīna has the faʿīla pattern and the plural mudun.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī gives the morphological pattern and plural."}, {"id": "18:19/q53/p2", "position": "It derives from dāna or dīn, denoting obedience or rule over inhabitants.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports Qutrub deriving it from dāna; Ibn Fāris connects dīn with obedience to a governor or a people's subjection to a ruler. {"id": "18:19/q54", "question": "Why do the commands use fāʾ for the errand's steps but wāw for gentleness?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "18:19/q54/p1", "position": "Fāʾ orders dispatch, inspection and bringing food as successive steps; wāw adds gentleness because it is not a consequence of obtaining food.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān and al-Itqān explicitly contrast the ordered fāʾ clauses with the final wāw."}]}
